p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Much of what we do each day is not decided at all. We take the same route to work, reach for the same seat at the table and accept the settings that came with a new phone, not because we have weighed the alternatives but because the choice was made once and has since been running on its own. Psychologists describe such behaviour as habitual, and they have found that it is triggered less by intention than by context: the place, the time and the preceding action cue the response before any deliberate thought occurs.

This finding has an uncomfortable implication for anyone who hopes to change by willpower alone. Resolving to eat less or to read more is a matter of intention, but the old habit is tied to the old context, and so it reasserts itself as soon as attention lapses. People who succeed in changing their behaviour tend instead to alter their surroundings. They keep the biscuit tin out of sight, place the book on the pillow, or attach the new action to an existing routine, so that one cue now leads to a different response. Seen in this light, a habit is neither a vice nor a virtue in itself; it is an economy of the mind, freeing attention for matters that genuinely need it. The task is not to abolish habits but to arrange for good ones.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: In an age when almost any fact can be summoned on a telephone screen, the public library is often described as a relic, a building kept open out of sentiment rather than need. This view mistakes what libraries have always done. Their value never lay solely in the books on their shelves; it lay in offering a quiet and free space where anyone, regardless of income, could sit and think without being asked to buy anything. For a student whose home has one room and five occupants, the reading hall may be the only place where sustained concentration is possible. For an elderly pensioner, it may be the only public room in which he is welcome to linger.

The arrival of digital information has, if anything, enlarged this role. A screen offers abundance but not guidance, and the skill of judging which sources deserve trust is not acquired automatically. A trained librarian who can steer a reader from rumour towards reliable evidence performs a service that no search engine has replaced. When municipal budgets tighten, libraries are frequently the first institutions to lose staff and hours, precisely because their benefits are diffuse and difficult to count. Yet a society that closes them saves very little money and loses one of the few spaces in which citizenship, rather than purchasing power, is the only qualification for entry.

questions.q: Which is the most suitable title for the passage?
opts: The Unlimited Power of Willpower
Why All Habits Are Harmful
Changing Habits by Changing Context
How Phones Shape Our Choices
questions.why: Main idea: habits are cued by context, so successful change comes from altering surroundings.

questions.q: According to psychologists, habitual behaviour is triggered mainly by:
opts: A deliberate weighing of alternatives.
The place, the time and the preceding action.
The strength of a person's willpower.
The advice of friends and family.
questions.why: Detail: 'triggered less by intention than by context: the place, the time and the preceding action'.

questions.q: A person who resolves to exercise every morning but changes nothing else in his routine is, according to the passage, most likely to:
opts: Find the old routine returning as soon as his attention slips.
Find that exercise becomes automatic at once.
Lose all his other habits as well.
Succeed, since intention controls habitual behaviour.
questions.why: Inference: 'the old habit is tied to the old context, and so it reasserts itself as soon as attention lapses'.

questions.q: The examples of the biscuit tin and the book on the pillow are given to show that:
opts: Successful changers reshape their surroundings to support new behaviour.
Reading in bed is a harmful habit.
Willpower alone is enough to change behaviour.
Certain foods should be avoided at night.
questions.why: Purpose: they follow 'People who succeed in changing their behaviour tend instead to alter their surroundings'.

questions.q: In the phrase "an economy of the mind", the word "economy" most nearly means:
opts: Efficient saving of limited effort
Mean or miserly behaviour
A system of trade and money
The wealth of a nation
questions.why: Vocabulary: a habit is an economy because it is 'freeing attention for matters that genuinely need it'.

questions.q: The central argument of the passage is that public libraries:
opts: are valuable chiefly because of the rare books they preserve.
should be replaced by digital services to save public money.
have lost their purpose now that facts are available on phones.
remain valuable as free public spaces and sources of guidance despite digital information.
questions.why: Main idea: the author rejects the 'relic' view and says digital information 'has, if anything, enlarged this role'.

questions.q: According to the passage, why are libraries often the first to lose staff and hours when budgets tighten?
opts: Librarians lack the skills needed for digital information.
Their buildings are too costly to maintain.
Readers have largely stopped visiting them.
Their benefits are diffuse and difficult to count.
questions.why: Detail: 'precisely because their benefits are diffuse and difficult to count'.

questions.q: With which of the following statements would the author most likely agree?
opts: Libraries should charge entry fees in order to survive.
Easy access to information does not by itself give people the ability to judge it.
Students from crowded homes prefer to study at home.
Search engines have made trained librarians unnecessary.
questions.why: Inference: 'A screen offers abundance but not guidance, and the skill of judging which sources deserve trust is not acquired automatically.'

questions.q: The author's attitude towards those who call the library a relic is best described as:
opts: fully in agreement with their view.
indifferent to their opinion.
corrective, holding that they misunderstand what libraries do.
sympathetic, accepting that libraries are kept open out of sentiment.
questions.why: Tone: 'This view mistakes what libraries have always done.'

questions.q: As used in the passage, the word 'diffuse' means:
opts: spread thinly over many people rather than concentrated
temporary and short-lived
harmful and difficult to control
kept secret from the public
questions.why: Vocabulary: the benefits are 'diffuse and difficult to count' because they are spread across many users in small ways.
